about.sources: Church Latin, tier 2, is five traditional prayers: the Glory Be, the Hail Mary, the Hail Holy Queen through the versicle Ōrā prō nōbīs, the Apostles’ Creed, and the Angelus with its closing collect. The Latin is the public-domain traditional text in the wording of the appendix to the Compendium of the Catechism of the Catholic Church (2005): Et in Spīritum Sānctum, and dēscendit ad īnferōs. The same prayers are witnessed in the traditional collections at preces-latinae.org. Biblical lines were checked against the Clementine Vulgate (Luke 1:28, 1:38, 1:42, and John 1:14) and are not copied word for word from those verses. The English under each line is a new literal translation made for this app. Meal prayers, the Act of Contrition, and the Regina Caeli are not in this pack. From Easter to Pentecost the Angelus is replaced by the Regina Caeli; that prayer is only mentioned, not set out here.

lines.en: Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.
As it was in the beginning, and now and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen.
Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you.
Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb, Jesus.
Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen.

texts.title: Hail, Holy Queen: through the valley of tears

lines.en: Hail, Queen, mother of mercy; our life, sweetness, and hope, hail.
To you we cry, exiled children of Eve.
To you we sigh, groaning and weeping in this valley of tears.
Come then, our advocate, turn those merciful eyes of yours toward us.
And after this exile, show to us Jesus, the blessed fruit of your womb.
O gentle, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary.
Pray for us, holy Mother of God.
That we may be made worthy of the promises of Christ.

texts.title: The Apostles’ Creed: through the judgment

lines.en: I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth,
and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord,
who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary,
suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried,
descended to the dead below, on the third day rose from the dead,
ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty;
from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

texts.title: The Apostles’ Creed: the Spirit and the life to come

lines.en: And in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints,
the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and life everlasting. Amen.
The angel of the Lord announced to Mary.
And she conceived by the Holy Spirit.
Behold the handmaid of the Lord. Let it be done to me according to your word.
And the Word was made flesh.
And dwelt among us.
Let us pray.

Pour your grace into our minds, we beg, Lord, so that we, to whom the incarnation of Christ your Son was made known as an angel announced it, may be brought by his Passion and cross to the glory of the resurrection.
Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

lessons.title: Glory be
lessons.sum: Glōria Patrī et Fīliō et Spīrituī Sānctō.
lessons.lead: The Latin is the traditional prayer, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
Glōria is nominative. Patrī, Fīliō, Spīrituī Sānctō are dative: “glory to the Father, to the Son, to the Holy Spirit.” Fīliō is the dative of fīlius. Spīritus is 4th declension, so the dative is spīrituī.

Sīcut erat “as it was”: erat is the imperfect of sum. In prīncipiō and in saecula saeculōrum are “in the beginning” and “unto ages of ages.” This prayer uses no word that is not already in the deck.

lessons.title: The Hail Mary
lessons.lead: The Latin is the traditional prayer, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
Avē is the greeting “hail.” Grātiā plēna is “full of grace”: grātiā is ablative, and plēna agrees with Mary. Tēcum is tē plus cum, “with you.”

Benedicta and benedictus are from benedīcō. Tū is “you.” Frūctus ventris tuī is “the fruit of your womb”: ventris and tuī are genitive. Iēsus is nominative, naming that fruit.

The last sentence addresses Mary in the vocative: Sāncta Māria, Māter Deī. Ōrā is the imperative of ōrō. Peccātōribus is ablative plural, “for us sinners,” beside nōbīs. In hōrā mortis nostrae is “at the hour of our death.”
lessons.diff: Luke 1:28 in the Clementine Vulgate is Ave grātia plēna: Dominus tēcum: benedicta tū in mulieribus, without the name Mary. Luke 1:42 is benedicta tū inter mulierēs, and it does not add Iēsus. The prayer uses in mulieribus, adds Māria and Iēsus, and then the petition Sāncta Māria… ōrā prō nōbīs.

lessons.title: Hail, Holy Queen, part 1
lessons.lead: The Latin is the traditional prayer, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
Salvē is the same greeting as a fixed call, “hail,” said to Rēgīna and Māter in the vocative. Misericordiae is genitive, “of mercy.” Vīta, dulcēdō, et spēs nostra are nominative, in apposition: “our life, sweetness, and hope.”

Exsulēs fīliī Evae “exiled sons of Eve.” Evae is the genitive of Eva. A typed Hevae is accepted; the form that is shown is Evae. Exsulēs is the Church spelling. The spelling without s is still accepted, as with other exs- words, and it is not listed as a second form.

Gementēs et flentēs are present participles, “groaning and weeping,” agreeing with “we.” In hāc lacrimārum valle is ablative: “in this valley of tears.”

lessons.title: Hail, Holy Queen, part 2
lessons.sum: Ēia ergō, then Ōrā prō nōbīs.
lessons.lead: The Latin is the traditional prayer, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
Ēia ergō turns the prayer: “come, then.” Advocāta nostra is vocative, “our advocate.” Illōs tuōs misericordēs oculōs is the accusative object of converte, “turn those merciful eyes of yours.” Ad nōs is “toward us.”

Ostende is the imperative of ostendō. Iēsum benedictum frūctum is accusative, “Jesus, the blessed fruit.” Nōbīs is “to us.” Post hoc exsilium is “after this exile,” accusative after post. The shown spelling is exsilium.

Ō clēmēns, ō pia, ō dulcis are vocatives. The versicle is a wish: Ōrā “pray,” then ut dignī efficiāmur “that we may be made worthy,” with prōmissiōnibus Chrīstī in the ablative, “of the promises of Christ.”
lessons.diff: The same versicle, Ōrā prō nōbīs, sāncta Deī Genetrix, is said again in the Angelus. A longer prayer sometimes printed after the Salve is not part of this lesson.

qs: Post hoc exsilium: post takes the
a purpose clause, “that we may be made worthy”

lessons.title: The Apostles’ Creed, part 1
lessons.sum: From Crēdō in Deum through iūdicāre vīvōs et mortuōs.
lessons.lead: The Latin is the traditional prayer, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
Crēdō in plus the accusative is “I believe in”: Deum, Patrem, Creātōrem, Iēsum Chrīstum. Caelī et terrae are genitive, “of heaven and of earth.” Fīlium eius ūnicum “his only Son”: eius is the genitive of is, not a reflexive.

Conceptus est and nātus are perfect participles, “was conceived,” “born.” Passus, crucifīxus, mortuus, sepultus continue that list. Sub Pontiō Pīlātō is ablative. Dēscendit ad īnferōs is “went down to those below,” the masculine plural of īnferus used as a noun. Tertiā diē is ablative of time.

Ad caelōs is the Church plural “to heaven.” Ad dexteram is “at the right hand,” the Missal’s feminine of dexter. Ventūrus est “he is going to come,” and iūdicāre is the infinitive “to judge.”
lessons.diff: This is the Apostles’ Creed, not the Nicene Creed in the Mass lessons. The wording here is Et in Spīritum Sānctum, not a second Crēdō, and dēscendit ad īnferōs.

lessons.title: The Apostles’ Creed, part 2
lessons.sum: Et in Spīritum Sānctum, through vītam aeternam.
lessons.lead: The Latin is the traditional prayer, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
The sentence still depends on crēdō: “and (I believe) in the Holy Spirit.” Spīritum Sānctum is accusative. Then the objects stay accusative without another in: sānctam Ecclēsiam catholicam, sānctōrum commūniōnem, remissiōnem peccātōrum, carnis resurrectiōnem, vītam aeternam.

Sānctōrum is genitive plural, “of the saints,” with commūniōnem. Peccātōrum is “of sins.” Carnis is the genitive of carō, “of the flesh,” not a separate word for “body.” Vītam aeternam agrees in the feminine accusative.

lessons.title: The Angelus
lessons.sum: Angelus Dominī, three Hail Marys, and the collect.
lessons.lead: The Latin is the traditional prayer, with macrons added. The English is a literal translation.
lessons.notes:
The Angelus is three short verses, each followed by the Hail Mary, then the versicle, the collect, and the Glory Be. The Hail Mary and the Glory Be are the prayers you already have; they are not a second card.

Angelus Dominī nūntiāvit Māriae: Māriae is dative, “to Mary.” Concēpit is the perfect of concipiō. Ecce ancilla Dominī and fīat mihi secundum verbum tuum are Mary’s answer. Fīat is the subjunctive of fīō, “let it be done.”

Verbum carō factum est: factum agrees with Verbum, and carō is the nominative of “flesh.” Habitāvit in nōbīs “dwelt among us.” In the collect, īnfunde is the imperative “pour,” mentibus nostrīs “into our minds,” and Angelō nūntiante is an ablative absolute, “as an angel announced.” Perdūcāmur is “may we be brought.”
lessons.diff:
Luke 1:38 is Ecce ancilla Dominī: fīat mihi secundum verbum tuum. John 1:14 goes on, et vīdimus glōriam eius; the Angelus stops at habitāvit in nōbīs.

From Easter through Pentecost this devotion is replaced by the Regina Caeli. That prayer is not set out in this lesson.
